title: A way of thinking about subject leadership
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart sets out a mental model for subject leadership in primary schools, beginning from the premise that subject leadership should be collective rather than vested in one individual, both to manage workload and to protect a school from boom-and-bust cycles of staff turnover. He organises what subject leaders need to know around four anchoring concepts: curriculum choices, pedagogy and assessment as the 'what', and evaluation, prioritisation and development as the 'how'. On curriculum he stresses knowing why a published scheme was chosen and how it has been adapted, fleshing out substantive and disciplinary knowledge, curating resources and sequencing content across the age range. On assessment he elevates responsive teaching and iterative unit improvement while dismissing termly teacher assessments in foundation subjects as unreliable and wasteful. He argues that senior leaders must coordinate subject priorities to avoid confusion, and that subject leaders should align beliefs and shared language. Finally, he advises new subject leaders to build their own subject expertise first, since credibility to advise colleagues must be earned.
points: Hart frames subject leadership as shared knowledge and collective work, arguing that reliance on individual leaders leaves schools at the mercy of staff turnover.
His four anchoring concepts split into the 'what' (curriculum choices, pedagogy, assessment) and the 'how' (evaluation, prioritisation and development).
Subject leaders should own the adaptations to any published scheme and flesh out substantive knowledge, disciplinary knowledge and key concepts to reduce teacher workload.
He ranks responsive teaching and improving units for the next cohort above summative judgements, calling termly foundation-subject teacher assessments a significant waste of time.
New subject leaders are advised to spend their first months building subject expertise, because advising colleagues requires earned credibility.
quotes: Relying on individuals to lead subjects well without great systems or collaborative endeavours leaves a school vulnerable to boom and bust cycles at the mercy of staff turnover. As such, any reference to what a subject leader ought to know or do is less about the individual leading a subject but more about the collective leadership of that subject.

No scheme comes out of the packet and is perfect for any school community so a subject leader also needs to know about and influence adaptations to the published scheme. What have we changed? What have we dropped?

The order in which content is taught over the entirety of the primary age range can affect the extent to which it is understood. We might want increasing complexity as children get older or recurring themes.
Dylan Wiliam said that pedagogy trumps curriculum. Schools can never have the perfect curriculum and however well thought out ours is, it can be made or broken by how well it is taught.

I would argue that the most important form of assessment is the responsive teaching of noticing children’s responses and adapting either in the moment or the next part of the planned sequence. Depending on the subject, it may be that intervention is an option but there is one adaptation that might be better for long term school improvement and that is using information that we gather to make the unit of work better for the next cohort of children that study it; iterative improvement of content, sequencing and tasks.

If senior leaders don’t coordinate individual subject priorities, than we can easily find ourselves in a situation where we have too many and possible contradictory priorities which can create confusion, not cohesion. I’ve split this concept into aligning beliefs, anchoring concepts and a shared language.

At some point they will need to advise colleagues and that can only be done from a position of expertise. Credibility is earned and taking the time here before jumping into other subject leader activities can help to build trust too.
